basics.name: The Kinematics of Machinery: Outlines of a Theory of Machines (Franz Reuleaux; German original 'Theoretische Kinematik', 1875)
basics.url: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Kinematics_of_Machinery (full public-domain transcription of the 1876 English edition, with the scanned pages). Scans: https://archive.org/details/kinematicsofmach00reulrich (English, 1876), https://archive.org/details/theoretischekin00reulgoog (German, 1875)
basics.cost: Free (public-domain scans and transcription). The 1963 Dover reprint may still be found second-hand [uncertain]
basics.license: Public domain. The 1876 Macmillan English translation (Alexander B. W. Kennedy) and the 1875 German original are both out of copyright; Wikisource marks the original PD-old worldwide and the translation public domain in the US (published before 1931; translator died 1928). The Wikisource transcription text is offered under CC BY-SA, but the underlying work is public domain. What this means for the encyclopedia: text and figures can be quoted, reproduced and adapted freely
basics.language: German original (1875); English translation (1876); French translation 'Cinematique: principes fondamentaux d'une theorie generale des machines' (1877)
basics.year: 1875 (German, F. Vieweg und Sohn, Braunschweig, with a separate atlas of plates); 1876 (English, Macmillan, London); 1877 (French). Second volume 'Die praktischen Beziehungen der Kinematik zu Geometrie und Mechanik' (Lehrbuch der Kinematik, Vol. 2) in 1900. Latest edition: Dover unabridged and corrected reprint of the 1876 English edition, 1963
basics.access_barrier: none (free scans on the Internet Archive and Cornell eCommons, free transcription on Wikisource). The Dover 1963 reprint on the Internet Archive is lending-library only
basics.image_license: Public domain (19th-century woodcut figures and plates). 59 figures are already extracted on Wikimedia Commons in 'Category:Images from The Kinematics of Machinery (1876)', and the whole scan is there as a DjVu file
basics.authority_level: academic: the founding text of the theory of machines by Franz Reuleaux ('father of kinematics'), director of the Berlin Gewerbe-Akademie; a classic, historically authoritative, not peer-reviewed in the modern sense

coverage.covers: A theory of machines rather than a catalogue. It introduces pairs of elements (kinematic pairs: lower pairs with surface contact, higher pairs with line or point contact), incomplete pairs closed by force (springs, gravity), flexible elements (tension organs such as belts, ropes and chains, and pressure organs such as fluids), kinematic chains and their inversions, dead points, and a symbolic notation for mechanisms. It then analyses crank chains (four-bar, slider-crank, double slider, conic chains), about 30 named rotary pumps and blowers (chamber-crank and chamber-wheel trains, e.g. Root's blower, Pappenheim wheels), the constructive elements of machines (screws, keys, rivets, pins, shafts, couplings, belts, gears, flywheels, crossheads), click-gear (pawls), ratchet trains, locks as ratchet trains (Chubb, Bramah, Yale), brakes, engaging and disengaging gear, valves, springs, complete machines, and kinematic synthesis (screw chains, wheel chains, planet-wheel trains, cam trains, pulley chains). About 440 text figures [uncertain], 13 chapters, 162 numbered sections
coverage.organisation: By theory, chapter by chapter: general outlines, phoronomics (relative motion, centroids), pairs of elements, incomplete pairs, incomplete chains, history, kinematic notation, kinematic analysis, chamber-crank trains, chamber-wheel trains, constructive elements, complete machines, kinematic synthesis. It is a treatise, not a look-up catalogue: there is a detailed contents list and an alphabetical index, but no grouping by 'what do you need it to do'. Hard going for someone who doesn't know the terms, and much of the vocabulary is Victorian (e.g. 'click-gear', 'centroid', 'chamber-wheel train')
coverage.scope_match: medium. It founded the classification of connection types by how two parts touch and move (the kinematic pair), which is the backbone of any joint taxonomy, and it covers several in-scope families (pawls and ratchets, locks, brakes, clutches and couplings, planet-wheel trains, cams, belt and chain drives, springs). But it is theory-heavy, has no maker content, and treats most items briefly as examples of the theory
coverage.taxonomy_used: Reuleaux's kinematic classification. (1) Pairs of elements: lower pairs (surface contact; the closed pairs are the screw, the turning pair and the sliding pair) versus higher pairs (line or point contact, e.g. gear teeth, cams, curves of constant breadth), plus force-closed and flexible (tension/pressure organ) pairs. (2) Kinematic chains: simple and compound, and their inversions (fixing different links). (3) Twelve class symbols for kinematic elements: S screw, R solid of revolution, P prism, C cylinder, K cone, H hyperboloid, G sphere (globe), A sector or arc, Z tooth or projection, V vessel or chamber, T tension organ, Q pressure organ, combined into formulas for chains and mechanisms. (4) A practical classification of constructive elements in three groups: I rigid elements (fastenings such as rivets, keys, strained joints and screwed joints, then pins, bearings, shafts, fixed couplings, levers, cranks, connecting rods, crossheads, friction wheels, toothed wheels, flywheels); II flectional elements (tension organs, pressure organs and their partners such as pipes, pistons, cylinders, stuffing boxes and valves, and springs); III trains (click-gear, brakes, moveable couplings and clutches). With the notation he showed that the four-bar linkage gives 54 mechanisms in 12 classes. The later Voigt model catalogue grouped Reuleaux's models into about 25 lettered classes (A-Z)
coverage.example_types: screw pair; turning (revolute) pair; sliding (prismatic) pair; higher pairs such as the Reuleaux triangle in a square (curve of constant breadth); force-closed pairs held by springs or gravity; slider-crank and its inversions (swinging block, turning block); double slider-crank (elliptic trammel, Oldham coupling); crossed slider-crank; parallel and anti-parallel cranks; conic (spherical) crank chains (Hooke's universal joint); Root's blower and other rotary pumps (chamber-wheel trains); click-gear, i.e. pawl and ratchet holding (push click and pull click); ratchet trains (intermittent one-way drive with retaining gear); locks as ratchet trains (Chubb, Bramah, Hobbs, Yale); brakes and brake gear; engaging and disengaging gear (clutches); escapements and 'curb-trains'; springs as constructive elements (tension, pressure, bending and twisting springs); Watt's planet-wheel (sun-and-planet) train; epicyclic chamber-wheel gear; cam pairs; screwed and keyed joints (fastenings as closed chains)
coverage.making_methods: General 19th-century mechanical engineering (machines, engines, pumps, locks). Not aimed at any modern making method
coverage.item_count: 13 chapters, 162 numbered sections, about 440 woodcut figures (the last figures are numbered in the mid-440s) plus plates [uncertain]; 12 element class symbols; 54 four-bar mechanisms in 12 classes. The companion model collection had about 800 models (Reuleaux's own), of which 368 were in the 1907 Voigt catalogue and 220 survive at Cornell
coverage.special_behaviours_covered: torque-limiting: no explicit coverage (brakes and friction clutches only) [uncertain]; self-locking: partly (click-gear 'holds fast' in one direction; brakes that stop a pair; screwed joints); hand-release only: partly (locks where the key lifts the click) ; one-way/ratchet: yes, in depth (click-gear, ratchet trains, reversed motion in free click trains); indexing/detent: partly (ratchet trains give intermittent motion; escapements); over-centre: partly (dead points in crank chains and how they are passed) - not as over-centre latches; compliant: partly (springs and 'flectional' elements as kinematic elements); print-in-place: no; gear trains/gearboxes: yes as theory (toothed-wheel pairs, wheel chains, Watt's planet train, epicyclic gear) but not gearbox design; powered connectors: no; adhesive types: no
coverage.entry_structure: Not entry-based. Each numbered section gives prose explanation, woodcut figures with lettered links, and the mechanism's symbolic formula (e.g. (C''3 P-) for a slider-crank chain), with historical notes and references to inventors and patents
coverage.audience_level: undergraduate / professional / research (19th-century engineering students and engineers); today mainly history of technology and kinematics researchers

usefulness.beginner_friendliness: low. Dense Victorian prose, symbolic formulas and specialist terms. It is valuable for its concepts (joint = pair, mechanism = chain) but not readable as a beginner's guide
usefulness.has_images: yes. Hundreds of clear 19th-century woodcut line figures plus plates (the German edition has a separate atlas of 8 folded plates, per the Internet Archive record). Public domain
usefulness.has_animations: no (book). Cornell's KMODDL and DMG-Lib show photos, GIFs and videos of the physical Reuleaux models that were made to accompany it
usefulness.gaps: Not a catalogue: no plain-English 'what is it for' grouping, no selection advice, no dimensions or design rules, no modern elements (snap fits, compliant or printed joints, quick-release hardware, powered latches, adhesives), old terminology, and the symbolic notation fell out of use after Reuleaux's death
usefulness.good_for_entry_links: medium to high. Wikisource has stable per-page URLs for every scanned page, e.g. https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Page:The_Kinematics_of_Machinery.djvu/478 (click-gear, push and pull clicks) and https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Page:The_Kinematics_of_Machinery.djvu/489 (locks as ratchet trains; brakes). Good for 'historic source' links on single entries such as ratchets, locks, Reuleaux triangle or slider-crank
usefulness.reusable_data: Fully reusable: the work and its figures are public domain. Structured access: Wikisource page-by-page wikitext (MediaWiki API), Wikidata item Q19091519, a DjVu scan and 59 extracted figures on Wikimedia Commons, and Internet Archive full-text OCR. The Cornell eCommons DSpace API exposes the German edition (Lehrbuch der Kinematik V.1 and V.2) and related KMODDL references
usefulness.maintained: Closed historical work (1875/1876, Vol. 2 1900). The online copies are well maintained: Wikisource page last edited January 2026 (most pages are still marked 'not proofread'); several Internet Archive scans; Cornell eCommons copies added 2018
usefulness.ideas_to_borrow: (1) Describe every connection as a 'pair': what the two contacting surfaces are and how they let the parts move (surface contact = lower pair, line/point contact = higher pair). This is a simple top-level question for the flow chart ('do the parts slide, turn, screw, roll or grip?'). (2) The idea of 'closure': a pair can be held together by its shape (form-closed), by a force such as a spring or gravity (force-closed), or by the rest of the chain. This maps directly onto snap fits, magnets and spring latches. (3) Treat fastenings as pairs that have been locked so they no longer move, putting fixed joints and moving joints on one scale. (4) His grouping of 'click-gear, brakes, couplings and clutches' as 'trains' that stop or start motion is close to the project's special behaviours (one-way, self-locking, hand-release). (5) Inversion: show how fixing a different part turns one chain into several mechanisms, a nice way to show relatives between entries
usefulness.design_rules_given: No numerical design rules (no clearances, fits, strengths or torques). It gives geometric methods (centroids, tooth profile construction, Willis's method) and kinematic analysis only
usefulness.file_formats: Book. Online: Wikisource HTML, EPUB, MOBI and PDF exports; Internet Archive PDF, DjVu, EPUB and OCR text; Commons DjVu and individual figure images
usefulness.terminology_value: high for the origin and history of core terms: kinematic pair, lower and higher pair, kinematic chain, inversion, closure, centroid (later 'centrode'), Reuleaux triangle, and for German-English equivalents (Kennedy's translation notes, e.g. his split of 'click-gear' for holding pawls vs 'ratchet-gear' for driving pawls). Some of its words are obsolete, so pair them with modern names
usefulness.decision_support: None. There is no selector or comparison. The notation and the synthesis chapter were meant as a systematic way to generate mechanism options, but they are theoretical, not a look-up tool
usefulness.derived_from_or_overlaps: Builds on earlier work on mechanisms, including Willis (whose tooth-profile method it uses, Section 36) and Reuleaux's teacher Redtenbacher, and reviews earlier classification and notation attempts in Section 53 'Former Attempts' [uncertain: which authors that section discusses was not checked]. It is the theory behind the Reuleaux model collection (about 800 models; Voigt catalogue 1907), and hence behind Cornell's KMODDL and DMG-Lib's Reuleaux models. Kennedy's own 'The Kinematics of Machinery: two lectures' (1881) and later texts (Burmester, Grübler, Hartenberg and Denavit 1964) spread its ideas. Artobolevsky's handbook uses the kinematic-pair idea it founded. Wikipedia's 'Kinematic pair' article is built on it
